fields.v: Tran, H., Nashold, L., Krishnan, R., Bigeard, A., Gu, A. (2026). Vibe Code Bench: Evaluating AI Models on End-to-End Web Application Development. In: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (CAIS '26), San Jose, CA, USA. ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/3786335.3813180. Read from arXiv:2603.04601v3 [cs.SE], 13 May 2026

Conference — CAIS '26 (ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems, San Jose), DOI 10.1145/3786335.3813180 (venue from the ACM export, slr/exports/acm-S2-2026-11-18.bib); full text read from arXiv:2603.04601v3 (access log: 'arXiv version of the DOI record')
Vals AI, San Francisco, USA (Tran, Nashold, Krishnan, Bigeard); Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA (Gu)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — Vibe Code Bench (VCB), a benchmark of 100 natural-language web application specifications with 964 browser workflows (10,131 substeps) scored by an autonomous browser agent; 16 frontier models compared in one OpenHands-based harness; evaluator-alignment study (cross-model and three human annotators) and variance analysis

No SDD approach. Configurations compared: a modified fork of OpenHands (VibeCodeBench-Openhands-Scaffold; no version stated) with 16 models: GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.2-Codex, GPT-5 Mini, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6 Thinking, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5 Thinking, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3.5 Plus Thinking, Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning, Kimi-K2.5 Thinking, MiniMax M2.5, GLM-5, DeepSeek V3.2 Thinking (model IDs in Table 15)

Per task, a concise natural-language application specification written from a non-technical perspective (overview, user roles, authentication, core features, content and constraints, primary user flows; example in App. H), shown to the model. A fixed system prompt (App. G) prescribes the stack (React + Vite, Tailwind CSS, Supabase; Express only if needed), Docker Compose deployment, migrations in supabase/migrations/, an idempotent seed routine, screenshots of self-testing, and two READMEs (TECHNICAL_README.md, USER_README.md). Workflow test definitions (6-23 per task) are benchmark artefacts used by the evaluator

Benchmark construction: idea generation; GPT-5 draft of specification and 6-23 UI workflows; two-pass human review by PM reviewers; audit (PM line review + LLM audit) and freeze. Generation: agent builds the app from the specification in an isolated container (scaffold, edit, database setup, app launch, browser self-test, submit) within up to 5 h. Evaluation: deployment verification; workflow execution by the Browser Use agent; workflow scoring (pass at >=90% substeps); application aggregation

Benchmark construction only: two PM reviewers edit and finalize each task (Accept/Modify/Reject per test), line review of each workflow before freeze. None during generation (the agent 'CANNOT interact with the user')
N/A (no SDD approach); the agent runs an autonomous end-to-end build from a natural-language specification
Not classifiable (benchmark of models building apps from natural-language specifications); authors do not use SDD terms, framing is 'vibe coding' / 'zero-to-one'
New project (greenfield, 'zero-to-one' web applications built from scratch)

100 specifications (50 validation, 50 test; results reported on the 50-task test split); 964 workflows, 10,131 substeps (test: 473 workflows, 5,136 substeps); 6-23 workflows per task; 28/100 apps need Stripe and/or email; up to 5 h generation per app. Size of generated code Not stated
Web applications: Individual (24), Solo Founder (45), Enterprise Tool (31); third-party services Stripe (payments) and MailHog email; Supabase backend
N/A (no developers; autonomous agent). Specifications reviewed by PMs; human alignment study with three expert annotators (profile not detailed)

Total model API cost of generation per application (USD, native provider pricing, no discount, caching accounted); latency = end-to-end wall-clock generation time per application (min); evaluator cost per workflow quoted ($0.093 GPT-5.2, $1.48 Sonnet 4.6)

Accuracy = percentage of workflows passing per application (a workflow passes when >=90% of its substeps succeed), mean +/- SE over the 50 test applications; share of apps scoring zero / 100%; apps failing to start; accuracy by difficulty, integration and domain
None (code readability, design quality and security explicitly not measured)
None

Tool-call distribution per model (Table 8); browser calls per app and Pearson correlation with accuracy (r=0.72; partial r=0.72 controlling for latency; edit calls r=0.09); trajectory action composition; six-category error taxonomy of failed workflows; generation vs evaluator variance decomposition; pairwise step-level agreement between evaluators (model-model, model-human, human-human)

Automatic: Browser Use agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5 (vision, headless 1920x1200, max 100 steps per workflow) executes the pre-authored workflows on the deployed app and returns LLM-as-judge substep pass/fail; cost and latency from generation runs. Manual: human alignment study (18 apps, 1,401 substeps, two of three blind human evaluators per app). Method used to assign the error taxonomy Not stated

Criterion: none stated by the authors for a configuration (a workflow passes at >=90% substeps; accuracy = % workflows passed). Values on the test split (Table 4): accuracy +/- SE; mean cost USD per app; mean latency. One generation per app; quality verdict and cost verdict for every entry: no criterion stated by the authors.

Tasks: VCB test split (50 specifications, 473 workflows). Configurations: 16 models from 9 providers in the same OpenHands-based harness. Baseline: none (models ranked against each other). Held constant: harness, system prompt, mandated tech stack, 22 tools, containerised environment with Supabase/MailHog/Stripe, wall-clock budget up to 5 h per app, retry policy, evaluator (Browser Use + Claude Sonnet 4.5, 100 steps, pass at >=90% substeps). Varied per model to elicit best performance: temperature, top-p, highest reasoning level; vision unavailable for GLM-5, MiniMax M2.5, DeepSeek V3.2. Acceptance tests: pre-authored browser workflows reviewed by PMs, judged by the LLM browser agent; checked against human annotators. Repetitions: one generation per app per model in the main results; variance panel of 6 apps x 3 models x 5 generations and 5 evaluator reruns. Human intervention: none

GPT-5.3-Codex best (61.8%), then Claude Opus 4.6 (57.6%), GPT-5.2 and Opus 4.6 Thinking (53.5%), Sonnet 4.6 (51.5%); open-weight models 15-24% (GLM-5 23.4%); lowest Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning (1.2%). Gap MiniMax M2.5 vs Opus 4.6: 2.8% on SWE-Bench vs 42.7% on VCB. Higher cost and latency associated with higher accuracy with diminishing returns; Opus 4.6 near-top accuracy at lower cost and latency than GPT-5.3-Codex. Browser calls per app correlate with accuracy (r=0.72). All-model average falls from 34.18% (no integration) to 13.49% (email + Stripe), and from 44.29% (easy) to 21.36% (medium) to 6.03% (hard). Top-5 models: 12.8% of apps score zero vs 73.2% for bottom-5; 14.0% of bottom-5 apps fail to start. Only SE reported, no significance tests; authors say near-tie differences require caution

Distinguished models strongly (1.2-61.8%), more than SWE-Bench. Repeatability: generation SE 3.47-5.00 points vs evaluator-rerun SE 0.99-3.00 on the 6-app panel; 73.5-92.5% of variance from generation; authors conclude major rankings are robust, near-ties need caution. Evaluator choice matters: GPT-5.2 agrees 33.1-38.8% with other model evaluators and 36.1% with humans, Claude Sonnet 4.5 86.4% with humans; human-human 88.6-93.6%. Limitations of the method stated: single harness, single tech stack, web applications only, code/design quality not measured

Limitations: design and code quality (readability, security, documentation, visual design) not measured; single OpenHands-based harness (other harnesses may score higher); single stack (React/Vite + Supabase); web applications only. Gaps: reliable end-to-end application development remains unsolved; improvement comes mainly from fewer complete failures; self-testing associated with success; evaluator choice should be a first-class reporting concern; 'zero-to-one' for CLI, desktop and mobile apps unexplored

Inconsistency: the validation split is called 'private validation' in the abstract and text (p. 1, 3) but 'Validation (public)' in Table 3 (p. 4); the ACM abstract in the queue says '50 public validation'. Section headings out of order in the extracted text (5.2 before 5/5.1, p. 7). Validation-split results not reported. Vision disabled for three models, so conditions are not fully identical. Tech stack mandated in the system prompt after preliminary runs. Replication: modified OpenHands scaffold and all trajectories and generated apps on GitHub (vals-ai); system prompt, example spec and tests in App. G-I; test split held out. No pre-registration. Programming languages: JavaScript/TypeScript (React + Vite, Node/Express), SQL (Supabase/PostgreSQL)
